h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: sklearn scales the L2 gradient by alpha/batch_size and applies it every step, so tiny batches turn an alpha increase into far stronger effective shrinkage and underfitting.
At tiny learning rates the net is undertrained and extra width speeds function-space progress per step, so widening helps most there.
Under strong L2 each extra penalized layer shrinks the signal multiplicatively, pushing deeper nets toward constant predictions.
Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs, so larger steps compensate and the optimal lr shifts upward.
Deeper ReLU stacks compound update magnitudes across layers and diverge at smaller learning rates, so raising lr hurts them more.
Very wide nets have surplus capacity that overfits small tabular datasets, so extra penalty is less harmful or even beneficial for them.
Single-hidden-layer nets get all their capacity from width, so widening yields larger gains than in deeper nets that already have representational slack.
At tiny learning rates training is step-limited, so cutting the number of updates by enlarging batches leaves the net badly undertrained.
Extra layers pay off only when lr is large enough to train them yet small enough to avoid divergence, which is the mid band.
Under standard parameterization, wide layers change outputs more per step, so they hit the instability threshold at lower lr and raising lr hurts them more.
